rv.q: Marianne Elliott’s production pulls these complex elements together with dazzling success.
If there’s a better, more vital way to honor the late, incomparable Stephen Sondheim than Marianne Elliott’s superb production of Company, Broadway hasn’t invented it.
"Company" is the best of what Broadway
It infuses new life into a classic show with such intelligence, wit and care that it could, and should, become a template for future productions.
In director Marianne Elliott’s exuberant, re-gendered staging, material and moment have been reconciled to smashing effect.
LuPone steals the show as Joanne, the bitter, boozy wife who delivers the musical's most famous number, 'The Ladies Who Lunch,' with a glass of liquor perpetually in hand.
This first major stage revival of a Sondheim work
These aren’t nullifying dissents by any means, not when the production itself keeps Sondheim’s flame so imaginatively alive.
Either way, there’s no question that this revival is a perfect match for the Broadway moment.

So yes, I had sharply mixed feelings about this “Company,” but I still got much pleasure out of it—and it was a comfort to be able to see it at a moment when those of us who love Stephen Sondheim’s work are bereft at his passing.
I hate to put so much pressure on a single line, but this gesture betrays the thinness of Elliott’s thinking.

As directed by Marianne Elliott, however, in a gender-flipped version abetted by Sondheim himself, what was once the story of a man who is terrified of intimacy becomes something much less interesting: the story of a woman who is justifiably tired of her friends.
Hers is a prayer—she’s on her knees for at least one verse—and a song of surrender.
One unexpected side effect of the Bobbie transformation: the sudden stinging nature of “The Ladies Who Lunch,” which LuPone shakes and stirs and serves with icy perfection, all to a jazzy beat.
This new Company is so good, you can’t help thinking that it might work better than the original.
This gender-swapped revival of Company breathes new life into Sondheim's masterpiece, with Katrina Lenk delivering a powerhouse performance
This is the best cast on Broadway, bar none, and the great time they're palpably having jumps across the footlights and into the house.
Even when the gender switching feels less than completely thought out, the musical proves to be sturdy enough to allow for such noodling around without undermining the essence of the show.
Marianne Elliott’s brilliant update of Company makes this look and sound like a brand new show.

A miscast Bobbie aside, there is very little to complain about in this excellent production of one of Sondheim’s most dynamic works, created at a time when the writer-composer was transitioning from the Golden Age that raised him into the postmodern theatre he helped create.
When a director’s concept is this revelatory, bring on the deconstruction!

The reimagined Company plays perfectly into the dichotomy that comes along with any relationship or contemplation of singledom and brings the audience on a journey of all the sorrow, gratitude, regret, and happiness that a relationship can bring.
And this production is never better than when it dives headfirst into that joy:
Relying upon sex smirks and curious glances, Lenk gives a passive, barely passable performance in which a great production seems to operate around her instead of with her.

"The dreamlike set design by Bunny Christie, when working, beautifully plays on the coming-of-age search for self, inspired by the childlikeness of Alice In Wonderland. Bobbie’s home is contained in a box that emulates the bite-sized square footage of real NYC apartments.
This Company has been elevated, and I hope it never comes back down.
Elliott's creative team and otherwise delightful cast prove that Company can be glorious, even without a vibrant center to hold it together.
But the biggest glitch is the revival’s star Katrina Lenk, who was wonderful in Indecent and won a Tony for playing the world-weary tavern owner in The Band’s Visit.

cn.t: Critics praise Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped revival as a vital, dazzling tribute to Sondheim, with stellar direction and design making the 1970 musical feel fresh and modern, though some find lead Katrina Lenk underwhelming.

sg.ra: Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs orchestra floor is raked and the house has a single balcony (not two), so Center Orchestra rows A-D get close detail without the second-balcony crush. Playbill's Outsiders guide names Orchestra C Row B Seat 112 the best seat in the house; SeatPlan and Headout both call rows A-D the premium pick for plays specifically. Row numbering 101-114 (center block) means 107/108 sit dead-center on the aisle.

Multiple guides single out Center Orchestra rows F-K as the Jacobs value play: same centered sightline as the A-D premium block, but priced well below because Row I is where the mezzanine overhang line starts (overhead, not yet cutting into the stage). The Jacobs' single-balcony design and raked orchestra floor keep these rows clear, and Wikipedia notes two columns at the rear-of-orchestra promenade supporting the balcony - those sit behind Row N/O, so F-N stay clear of the columns.

SeatPlan and Headout both say the mezzanine overhang 'cuts into the top of the stage' starting at Row O - this is the Jacobs' specific geometry (mezz front at Row I, stage-top cutoff at Row O). Wikipedia adds that the rear-orchestra promenade has two columns supporting the balcony, so patrons here also share space with structural posts. Wheelchair spaces are assigned to rows I, J, P, and R per Headout, confirming P/R are flat promenade rows.

sg.vl: Fine if you pick single-digit seats
sg.ra: Side orchestra uses odd 1-27 (Left) and even 2-28 (Right). SeatPlan notes sightline restrictions intensify at double-digit seats (far aisle) and in back rows. Playbill's Outsiders guide specifically flagged that the right-side front rows were 'a clearer view' than left, because the show's tire set piece on house-left obstructs Orchestra L front rows - this is show-dependent but illustrates the Jacobs' shallow thrust style where side props block near side-orch seats. An AVFMS Orchestra G17 reviewer wrote 'sometimes the boxes block your view of the jungle gym' - the side boxes eat into side-orch sightlines.

sg.vl: Sharp angle, sells as obstructed for a reason
sg.ra: The Jacobs has 2 box seats on each side (16 total per Wikipedia) elevated beside the orchestra. TripAdvisor's theatre rep confirmed obstructed-view seats cluster 'on the extreme sides of the front mezzanine and orchestra' - the boxes are the prime example. Multiple guides warn boxes 'cut off high center stage scenes' and block views of stage-left from the right box / stage-right from the left box. SeatPlan explicitly recommends left boxes over right because the right box loses more stage-left content.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, 9 rows from stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Mezz rows A-B the best mezz view in the Jacobs; an AVFMS reviewer at Mezz A107 wrote 'you are perfectly centered and at only nine rows from the stage' - the Jacobs' single-balcony design (per Wikipedia, no second balcony) means the mezz sits close rather than stacked high. Row B dodges Row A's safety-bar issue that SeatPlan calls 'obstructive to shorter patrons.' Front mezz is 168 seats in rows A-D with premium centered sightlines on the full set.

sg.vl: Row E is the legroom hack
sg.ra: Rear mezz is 252 seats in rows E-K. The Jacobs-specific quirk: Row E sits directly behind the front-mezz cross-aisle with a curtain/bannister (not a wall), giving 'extra space' for taller patrons per SeatPlan - Playbill's Outsiders guide confirms Mezz Left Row E has 'a curtained divider between the aisle and row' for extra legroom. Rows G-K are flagged as value seats because the mezz has a 'good rake' and Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs has only one balcony so even Row K stays surprisingly close. An AVFMS Mezz H22 reviewer noted 'legroom is not great' - stick to Row E or aisle seats.
